```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Options to have images saved in the post folder
# And to disable symbols before output
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = "", comment = "")

# knitr hook to make images output use Hugo options
knitr::knit_hooks$set(
  plot = function(x, options) {
    hugoopts <- options$hugoopts
    paste0(
      "`{{< figure src=",
      '"', x, '" ',
      if (!is.null(hugoopts)) {
        glue::glue_collapse(
          glue::glue('{names(hugoopts)}="{hugoopts}"'),
          sep = " "
        )
      },
      ">}}`{=html}\n"
    )
  }
)

# knitr hook to use Hugo highlighting options
knitr::knit_hooks$set(
  source = function(x, options) {
  hlopts <- options$hlopts
    paste0(
      "```r ",
      if (!is.null(hlopts)) {
      paste0("{",
        glue::glue_collapse(
          glue::glue('{names(hlopts)}={hlopts}'),
          sep = ","
        ), "}"
        )
      },
      "\n", glue::glue_collapse(x, sep = "\n"), "\n```\n"
    )
  }
)

options(cli.num_colors = 1, width = 80)
```

The Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics ([IBGE](https://www.ibge.gov.br/en/))
produces Brazil's official statistics: the demographic census, the IPCA
inflation index, municipal GDP, and dozens of recurring economic, social and
agricultural surveys. Their results are published as thousands of aggregate
tables in SIDRA, IBGE's data retrieval system, and exposed through the
[IBGE Aggregates API](https://servicodados.ibge.gov.br/api/docs/agregados?versao=3).

[ibger](https://docs.ropensci.org/ibger/) is an R client for that API. It lets
you discover tables, inspect their metadata, and retrieve data as tidy
tibbles. The package recently passed
[rOpenSci software peer review](https://github.com/ropensci/software-review/issues/787),
and version 0.2.1 is on CRAN:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("ibger")
```

ibger grew out of everyday work. We are part of the Strategic Monitoring
Data Science Team of the Pernambuco state government, in northeastern
Brazil, which builds R-based tools to monitor state public
policies[^1]. Our dashboards and reports draw on IBGE indicators, and they
are updated by scripts that pull the same tables again and again, often for
every municipality and for many years at once. We wanted that access to be
scripted, validated and reproducible, rather than a series of manual
downloads from the SIDRA website. A few weeks after the first CRAN
release, [Daniel Vartanian](https://github.com/danielvartan) opened an
[issue](https://github.com/ropensci/ibger/issues/1) explaining that he
split his calls into smaller chunks by hand to get around the API's
limits, and suggested submitting the package to rOpenSci. Both ideas
stuck.

This tech note is about one problem that every heavy user of the API runs
into sooner or later: the limit on how many values a single request can
return, and how ibger works around it.

## The request limit

Each SIDRA table crosses variables, periods, geographic units and
classification categories, so results grow multiplicatively. A modest
question such as "how much soybean did each of Brazil's 5,570
municipalities produce in each year since 2000?" already means more than
140,000 values.

The API documentation states a limit of 100,000 values per request. In
practice, requests start to fail well before that: while developing ibger we
saw a request for 44,560 values succeed and one for 50,130 values fail. And
when a request is too large, the API does not say so. It answers with a
generic HTTP 500 error.

Here is what happens if we send the soybean query in a single request, with
automatic splitting turned off (`chunk = FALSE`). We use table 1612
(municipal crop production), variable 214 (quantity produced), category 2713
of classification 81 (soybeans) and the municipal level `"N6"`:

```{r fail, error=TRUE, message=FALSE}
library(ibger)

soy <- ibge_variables(
  1612,
  variable = 214,
  periods = 2000:2025,
  localities = "N6",
  classification = list("81" = 2713),
  chunk = FALSE
)
```

The usual workaround is to split the query by hand into several smaller
requests, guess sizes that will work, and bind the results back together.
ibger does this for you.

## Estimating the size before asking

Before sending a data request, ibger estimates the size of the result as the
product of the number of variables, periods, localities and categories
involved. Most of the numbers come straight from the arguments. The ones
that do not, such as "all municipalities" or "the last six periods", are
resolved from the table metadata: `ibge_metadata()` lists a table's
variables and classifications, and the period and locality endpoints list
what each table covers. These lookups are cached, so each one is made only
once per table in a session.

The same metadata powers ibger's validation: invalid variables, periods,
geographic levels or categories are caught before any data request is sent,
with an error that lists the allowed values.

## Splitting the request

If the estimate exceeds the limit, ibger splits the query into chunks:
first by periods and then, if a single period is still too large, by
localities. Locality chunks are also capped at 500 codes per request to keep
URLs at a safe length. Each chunk is requested in turn and the results are
combined into a single tibble.

With the default `chunk = TRUE`, the same soybean query just works:

```{r soy}
soy <- ibge_variables(
  1612,
  variable = 214,
  periods = 2000:2025,
  localities = "N6",
  classification = list("81" = 2713)
)

soy
```

The estimate was 26 periods × 5,564 municipalities, about 145,000 values,
so ibger fetched 8 years per request in four requests.

If you need smaller requests, for example on an unstable connection, pass
your own limit, as in `chunk = 20000`. With `chunk = FALSE` the query is
sent as is.

## From values to a picture

The `value` column is character, because IBGE uses special codes for
values that are zero after rounding (`-`), not applicable (`..`), not
available (`...`) or suppressed for confidentiality (`X`).
`parse_ibge_value()` converts them to numbers or `NA`. With that, the
145,000 values summarise into a picture of two decades of soybean expansion
in Brazil:

```{r soy-plot, message=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, hugoopts=list(alt="Two line charts for 2000 to 2025. Left: the number of municipalities producing soybeans grows from about 1,450 to about 2,640. Right: Brazilian soybean production grows from about 33 to about 165 million tonnes.", caption="Soybean production and producing municipalities in Brazil, 2000 to 2025 (IBGE, Produção Agrícola Municipal, table 1612).")}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

by_year <- soy |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(period),
    tonnes = parse_ibge_value(value)
  ) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    `Production (million tonnes)` = sum(tonnes, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6,
    `Producing municipalities` = sum(tonnes > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-year)

ggplot(by_year, aes(year, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#2a7f62") +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Production grew about fivefold over the period, while the number of
producing municipalities nearly doubled, from about 1,450 to over 2,600.

## Learning more

ibger also translates URLs from the legacy SIDRA API, such as those
produced by the SIDRA Query Builder or used in existing scripts, into
equivalent calls with `parse_sidra_url()` and `fetch_sidra_url()`, and ships
an interactive Shiny explorer for browsing the table catalog
(`ibge_explorer()`). The
[getting started vignette](https://docs.ropensci.org/ibger/articles/getting-started.html)
and the vignette on
[the concepts behind the IBGE API](https://docs.ropensci.org/ibger/articles/api-concepts.html)
are good places to start. If you work in Python, the sibling package
[ibgepy](https://strategicprojects.github.io/ibgepy/) offers the same
functions.
